title: Compiler Optimizations
summary: The standard passes that turn correct-but-naive IR into fast code — constant folding, dead code elimination, common subexpression elimination, inlining, and loop transformations — and the one rule every one of them must obey.

slides.markdown:
[intermediate-representations](intermediate-representations) built an IR specifically so optimizations have a tractable shape to operate on. This topic is what actually runs on that shape: a handful of standard passes — constant folding, dead code elimination, common subexpression elimination, inlining, loop transformations — each individually simple, each earning real, measurable speedups, and each governed by one non-negotiable rule.

That rule: every optimization must preserve **observable behavior**. An optimizer is free to change *how* a computation happens as long as it can't change *what the program visibly does* — same output, same side effects, same crashes on the same inputs. Every pass in this topic is really just "find work that provably doesn't affect observable behavior, then remove or reorder it."

**Constant folding**: if an expression's operands are all known at compile time, compute the result then and skip doing it at runtime. `x = 2 + 3` becomes `x = 5` — the addition simply never happens when the program runs.

**Constant propagation**: if a variable is known to always hold a specific constant value at some point, replace uses of that variable with the constant directly, which often *creates* new folding opportunities. `y = x + 1` where `x` is known to be `5` becomes `y = 5 + 1`, which folding then reduces to `y = 6`. The two passes feed each other — propagation exposes more foldable expressions, folding produces more known constants to propagate — which is why compilers typically run them in a loop together until neither finds anything new to do.

**Dead code elimination** removes computations whose results are provably never used — an assignment to a variable that's overwritten before being read, a whole branch of an `if` whose condition just got constant-folded to always-false, a function that's unreachable from any entry point.

This pass has real compounding value with the ones around it: constant folding can reduce `if (false)` from a condition that used to depend on a variable, and dead code elimination then deletes the entire now-unreachable branch, sometimes including further computations that only that branch used — which can, in turn, make *those* computations' inputs dead too, cascading. A single small optimization opportunity can unlock a chain of eliminations well beyond what it looks like from the original source.

If the exact same expression is computed more than once with none of its inputs changing in between, **common subexpression elimination (CSE)** computes it once and reuses the result. `y = a * b + c; z = a * b - d` computes `a * b` twice; CSE recognizes the repeated subexpression, computes it into one temporary, and reuses that temporary in both places.

This is exactly the pass [intermediate-representations](intermediate-representations) used as the motivating example for why an IR (basic blocks, explicit data flow) beats optimizing the raw AST directly — recognizing "is this expression already available" is straightforward on a flat instruction sequence with clear reachability, and much harder to reason about across an arbitrarily nested tree.

slides.sectionTitle: Inlining: trading size for removing call overhead
slides.markdown:
**Inlining** replaces a function call with a copy of the called function's body directly at the call site. This removes real call overhead (setting up the calling convention, jumping, returning) and — critically — exposes the inlined code to every *other* optimization running on this pass, since the caller's context (specific argument values, surrounding control flow) is now visible right where the callee's body is, enabling folding and CSE opportunities that didn't exist when the call was opaque.

The cost is code size: every inline site duplicates the function body. Inlining a large function into many call sites can bloat the binary enough to hurt instruction-cache behavior — more code competing for the same fixed-size instruction cache means more cache misses overall, which can make a program *slower* despite removing call overhead everywhere. This is the central trade-off compilers' inlining heuristics have to balance: small, hot, frequently-called functions are the clear win; large, cold, rarely-called ones usually aren't worth inlining at all.

- **Loop-invariant code motion**: if a computation inside a loop produces the same result on every iteration (its inputs never change within the loop), hoist it out to run once, before the loop, instead of once per iteration.
- **Unrolling**: replicate the loop body multiple times per iteration of a shrunk loop, reducing how many times the loop-control overhead (incrementing a counter, checking a condition, jumping back) is paid relative to the actual work done.
- **Strength reduction**: replace an expensive operation with a cheaper one that produces the same result in this specific context — a classic case is replacing `i * 4` inside a loop where `i` increments by 1 each time with an accumulator that just adds `4` each iteration, trading a multiply for an add.

All three matter disproportionately because loop bodies run many times — an optimization that saves a handful of cycles per iteration compounds into a large real-world win once multiplied by the iteration count, which is exactly why loops get dedicated optimization passes that straight-line code doesn't.

slides.sectionTitle: A loop before and after optimization
slides.markdown:
```text
; before: naive translation
for i in 0..n:
    idx = i * 4          ; recomputed every iteration
    total = total + arr[base + idx]

; after: strength reduction + loop-invariant motion applied
offset = base           ; hoisted, computed once
for i in 0..n:
    total = total + arr[offset]
    offset = offset + 4  ; multiply replaced with an add
```

The multiply `i * 4` becomes an accumulated add across iterations — genuinely cheaper on essentially every real CPU — and `base` no longer gets re-added to `idx` inside the loop, since that part of the address computation doesn't actually depend on the loop variable's *current* value in a way that needs recomputing. Neither change alters what the loop computes; both change how cheaply it computes it.

slides.sectionTitle: Observable behavior is the line optimizations can't cross
slides.markdown:
Every optimization in this topic is only legal because it's provably invisible to the program's observable behavior — same outputs, same I/O, same crashes on the same inputs. The moment an optimization *could* change something observable, it's not a valid optimization anymore, it's a miscompilation, even if it happens to look harmless.

Two concrete lines that must never be crossed: reordering across genuine **I/O** (moving a `print` or file write relative to other operations can change what a user actually sees, in what order — a real, user-visible difference), and reordering or eliminating an access to a variable marked `volatile` (a signal to the compiler that this specific memory location can change for reasons the compiler can't see — a hardware register, a value another thread writes — so assuming it's safe to cache in a register or skip re-reading is exactly the kind of assumption that's valid for ordinary variables and invalid here). Optimizers are conservative specifically because getting this line wrong produces bugs that only show up under optimization, and are notoriously hard to reproduce in a debug build where the same optimization didn't run.

"The compiler removed my benchmark loop entirely" is dead code elimination doing exactly what it's designed to do: if a loop computes a result that's never actually used — a classic microbenchmark mistake is looping over a computation and never reading, printing, or otherwise using the accumulated result — the optimizer correctly proves the entire loop has no observable effect and deletes it. The benchmark then reports a suspiciously fast time because it's timing an empty loop, not the intended computation.

The standard fixes: make the result *observably* used — print it, return it from the function, or write it to a `volatile` sink specifically to defeat this optimization; or use a benchmarking library's dedicated "blackbox" utility (many languages have one, precisely for this problem) which is specifically designed to tell the optimizer "treat this value as used, even though I'm not going to do anything with it" without adding real overhead to what's being measured. This is one of the most common and instructive real-world encounters with dead code elimination — most engineers meet this optimization first through a broken benchmark, not through reading a textbook.

slides.sectionTitle: Optimizations compound, and sometimes fight each other
slides.markdown:
The passes in this topic aren't independent — they run in a pipeline, often repeated, because each one can expose new opportunities for the others (folding exposes dead code, inlining exposes folding, CSE exposes more inlining candidates by shrinking code). Real compilers run these passes multiple times in sequence until a fixed point (nothing more changes) or a time budget runs out.

They can also work against each other: inlining and unrolling both increase code size and register pressure, which — connecting back to [code-generation](code-generation) — can push a function past the point where the register allocator has enough physical registers, forcing spills that eat into or even reverse the gain the optimization was chasing. This is why "more optimization passes" doesn't monotonically mean "faster code," and why real compilers expose optimization levels (`-O1`, `-O2`, `-O3`) that make different, deliberate trade-offs between how aggressively to chase gains that can sometimes backfire.

slides.sectionTitle: What optimization is, underneath the pass names
slides.markdown:
Strip away the individual pass names and every optimization in this topic is the same move: prove that some piece of work is redundant, unreachable, or reorderable without changing what the program can observably do, then exploit that proof to do less work or cheaper work. Constant folding, dead code elimination, CSE, inlining, and loop transformations are five different shapes of exactly that one idea, applied to five different kinds of redundancy.

This is also the entire reason optimizers are conservative rather than aggressive by default — a missed optimization opportunity costs performance; a wrongly-applied one costs correctness, and correctness always wins that trade. [interpreters-tree-walking-vs-bytecode](interpreters-tree-walking-vs-bytecode) picks the story back up from the execution side: what happens to code that skips this whole ahead-of-time optimization pipeline and gets interpreted instead.
